item.title: G7 to release 100 mln barrels of diesel over 4 months
item.description:
Published: 2026-10-03
PARIS, Oct. 2 (Xinhua) -- The Group of Seven (G7), in coordination with the International Energy Agency, will release up to 100 million barrels of diesel and other oil reserves over the next four months, according to a joint G7 leaders' statement released by the Elysee Palace on Friday. G7 leaders held a virtual meeting earlier in the day to address growing energy security challenges. According to the statement, the G7 will coordinate maintenance schedules across refineries to prevent simultaneous capacity shutdowns and temporarily increase utilization rates where feasible. The statement also reaffirmed the G7's commitment to refrain from export restrictions on energy and energy products between G7 countries and called on all producers to refrain from imposing bans that could exacerbate market tensions. French President Emmanuel Macron said after the meeting that the G7 had agreed not to impose export restrictions or bans among its members, noting that U.S. President Donald Trump had also been "very clear" on this point. These decisions "should bring down fuel prices," he added. ■

item.title: How Beijing channels lab breakthroughs onto production lines
item.description:
Published: 2026-10-03
BEIJING, Oct. 2 (Xinhua) -- Disc-shaped reels of iron-based superconducting tape, glinting with a metallic sheen, are sitting in the showroom of a company in Yizhuang, a high-tech zone in southeastern Beijing. The company, Guoke Superconductor, is building what it says is the world's first mass production line for such wire and tape, with an annual capacity of around 100 km, and expects to complete it by the end of 2026. "A fusion device needs 5,000 to 20,000 km of superconducting tape," said Zhang Xiaohu, the company's chairman, adding that the combined global capacity of all manufacturers in 2025 was not enough to support even one such device. Superconducting materials conduct electricity with zero resistance under specific conditions, including very low temperatures. They are foundational to fields such as controlled nuclear fusion, advanced medical equipment and quantum information, but stable production of long-length superconductors at scale has proved difficult. Founded in August 2025, Zhang's startup aims to take iron-based superconducting materials from the laboratory to industrial production, backed by Beijing's research institutes, high-end talent, and supportive advanced-manufacturing policies. Yizhuang, officially the Beijing Economic-Technological Development Area where the company is based, has given everything it needs to get off the ground. Covering 225 square km, or 1.37 percent of Beijing's land, Yizhuang contributed nearly 40 percent of the city's industrial added value, and its gross industrial output approached 700 billion yuan (about 104 billion U.S. dollars) last year. FROM LAB TO MASS PRODUCTION In a seven-story building at a cell therapy pilot base in Yizhuang, China's first approved stem cell drug is coming off a fully enclosed, automated production line. The drug, amimestrocel injection, was approved in 2025 for steroid-refractory acute graft-versus-host disease -- a complication of stem cell transplants in which the donor's immune cells attack the recipient's tissues and that does not respond to standard steroid treatment. It has saved more than 700 critically ill patients so far, according to its developer, Platinumlife Biotechnology (Beijing) Co., Ltd. "Once it enters the body, it is very much like a living drug factory, secreting active factors that promote tissue repair, mobilize the immune system and suppress inflammation," said Li Liang, the company's chief scientist. Yet making a scalable drug out of mesenchymal stem cells takes more than innovation alone. In 2022, Beijing brought the company to Yizhuang as a key project, enabling it to crack the hard nut. The company developed three-dimensional suspension bioreactors and fully automated, closed production lines to replace manual cell culture, achieving consistent quality among different drug batches and reducing the cost to one-seventieth of a comparable therapy approved in the United States. "We now have four production lines, each with an annual capacity of 40,000 to 50,000 bags," said Yin Rui, the company's chief marketing officer. A few kilometers away, a 24,000-square-meter "super factory" with 48 intelligent production lines is being built, due to start operating by the end of 2026 with a projected annual capacity of 5 million bags. "Yizhuang coordinates industrial space and provides special support for the construction of our super factory, including land guarantees, faster approvals and a dedicated task force. The project broke ground and had its main structure topped out in the same year, which greatly shortened the industrialization cycle," Yin said. EMPOWER ENTIRE SUPPLY CHAIN Speed is also on show at Xiaomi's car factory in Yizhuang, which took 14 months to go from project approval to completion. At full capacity, it can turn out a vehicle every 76 seconds. More than 1,000 robots work in the plant, where key processes such as die-casting, stamping, painting and final assembly are fully automated. Yizhuang is at the forefront of China's intelligent connected new energy vehicle industry, with innovation strength across vehicle design, manufacturing, chips, smart cockpits, and smart chassis. This gives Xiaomi a top-tier platform and intellectual support for technological innovation. In return, suppliers have grown alongside the carmaker. Beijing Hainachuan Automotive Parts Co., Ltd., a Yizhuang-based auto parts maker and Xiaomi's largest single supplier in the Beijing-Tianjin-Hebei region, had added nearly 14 billion yuan in output value across its upstream and downstream operations there thanks to Xiaomi's demand, its chairman, Li Jingang, said last November. Also in Yizhuang, Beijing Innovation Center of Humanoid Robotics Co., Ltd. formally launched a pilot-scale verification platform in January 2026, with a demonstration line for whole-robot production, a robot-joint production line and a small-batch trial line. It is open to companies, universities and research institutes, offering one-stop services from prototyping and process verification to assembly and testing. "The platform will give a strong boost to the high-quality development of China's humanoid robotics industry," said Li Chunzhi, COO of the company. POLICY SUPPORT Sustained policy backing underpins the fast growth of these companies. In the past five years, Yizhuang has issued nearly 70 policies supporting strategic emerging and future industries and set aside more than 10 billion yuan in industrial development funds each year, said Kong Lei, secretary of the area's Party working committee. In July, the area launched an instant-subsidy platform for "model vouchers," which help companies pay for AI model services. In June, Yizhuang's local state-owned investment firms launched four industrial investment funds totaling 20 billion yuan, covering AI and integrated circuits, biotechnology and health, intelligent manufacturing and robotics, and future industries. Over the next five years, Yizhuang will focus on next-generation intelligent manufacturing, Kong said. It will strengthen its leading industries such as integrated circuits, medicine and health, and intelligent connected vehicles, and develop future industries such as quantum information, biomanufacturing, brain-computer interfaces, and superconducting materials. By 2030, it aims to have eight industrial clusters worth more than 100 billion yuan each, with total industrial output value reaching 1 trillion yuan. Kong said the area will also raise the share of investment in basic research and open up application scenarios across the area, focusing on autonomous driving, robotics, aerospace technology, advanced energy and urban governance, to help move frontier technologies from laboratories into real-world use. Beyond Yizhuang, another part of Beijing is also drawing companies in growing numbers. In Tongzhou District, home to Beijing's municipal administrative center, the canal business district has attracted more than 20,000 registered companies. In the first half of 2026, it added 2,281 companies. Financial institutions, national high-tech enterprises, and firms that use specialized and sophisticated technologies to produce novel and unique products are increasingly gathering there. In Beijing, the distance between a laboratory bench and a production line has been compressed to a few kilometers. Technology, capital, land, talent, policy support and suppliers sit close enough to develop in step with one another -- that is what allows scientific discovery and industrial application to advance as a single process. ■

item.title: China's sea based rocket launches drive growth in commercial space industry
item.description:
Published: 2026-10-03
China's sea-based rocket launches are becoming more frequent and routine, injecting new momentum into the country's commercial space industry. Recently, the Gravity 1 carrier rocket successfully launched nine satellites into their planned orbits from waters off eastern China, setting new records for payload mass and orbital altitude in a single sea based launch. ■

item.title: Global humanitarian body sees China as key partner in building resilient African communities, says official
item.description:
Published: 2026-10-03
BEIJING, Oct. 3 (Xinhua) -- The International Federation of Red Cross and Red Crescent Societies (IFRC) sees China as an important partner in building durable solutions and community resilience in Africa, drawing on China's experience in poverty alleviation and community development, a humanitarian official said. Pierre Kremer, deputy regional director for Africa at IFRC, made the remarks in a recent interview with Xinhua on the sidelines of the Seminar on Resilient Community Building for Red Cross and Red Crescent Societies under the China-Africa Cooperation Framework in Beijing. Twenty-six representatives from national Red Cross and Red Crescent societies from 19 African countries, along with representatives of the IFRC, attended lectures, field visits and interactive discussions during the two-week seminar, exchanging experience and learning about China's practices in disaster risk reduction, community resilience and sustainable development. Hosted by the Training Center of the Red Cross Society of China and supported by the IFRC, the seminar provides a valuable platform for Chinese and African national Red Cross and Red Crescent societies to exchange expertise, share best practices and strengthen cooperation, said Kremer. Reviewing past cooperation between African national Red Cross and Red Crescent societies and Chinese partners, Kremer highlighted the Accelerating Malaria Elimination in The Gambia project as an effective example of partnership. The project was launched to accelerate malaria elimination in The Gambia by strengthening community-based prevention, early care-seeking and case management, alongside the procurement and distribution of seasonal malaria chemoprevention medicines for children under five. Kremer, who worked in China in 2021, said he had seen firsthand how community health systems could reach people effectively at the grassroots level. "I believe this experience could be valuable in building effective, people-centered and integrated community health workforces and systems in Africa." The malaria project also reflects a broader area of convergence between China's development cooperation in Africa and the IFRC's approach to humanitarian action: building local capacity and supporting sustainable development. The IFRC's Africa Zero Hunger initiative, for example, calls for a shift from short-term assistance toward longer-term resilience, with a focus on durable, locally led solutions that can be sustained and scaled up, he said. China's poverty alleviation efforts have offered another source of inspiration for this approach. "China's experience in building community resilience is even more valuable than funding," Kremer said, highlighting its know-how, multi-level leadership and consistent implementation. Looking ahead, the IFRC could provide a multilateral platform to help scale up effective China-Africa partnership programmes while strengthening and streamlining capacity-building efforts, particularly those aimed at developing the next generation of young leaders, he said. Youth leadership and entrepreneurship are areas where Kremer sees particular potential for cooperation. According to him, the IFRC's Africa region has around 4 million volunteers, 80 to 90 percent of whom are young people. Many of them work on the front lines of emergencies and take significant risks to serve their communities. "We want to give back by creating opportunities for them," Kremer said. "There is strong potential for cooperation with China in this area. We see an opportunity to combine the IFRC's network with China's expertise to support youth leadership and entrepreneurship in Africa." Digital transformation and renewable energy are other potential areas for cooperation, Kremer underlined. The IFRC is seeking to accelerate the digital transformation of its 16,000 branches across Africa, but only about 23 percent are currently connected. The goal is to connect all branches, particularly those in remote or conflict-affected areas, to strengthen emergency response and enable them to develop their own community information systems. "We want them to be fully self-reliant, autonomous and able to make decisions for themselves," Kremer said. Solar panels and other equipment are part of the solution, and so is building the capacity of volunteers to collect and use data from their own communities, said Kremer, noting that China could be a valuable partner in this effort, given its experience in community-level digital transformation and its globally competitive renewable energy technologies. "In the future, we look forward to further cooperation with Chinese partners through IFRC as a multilateral platform to scale up sustainable China-Africa cooperation projects to more countries," Kremer said.■

item.title: Feature: How Chinese robot dancers find their rhythm on American TV show
item.description:
Published: 2026-10-03
CHENGDU, Oct. 3 (Xinhua) -- A jade pendant bearing a small golden Sanxingdui mask rested against dancer Wu Yufei's chest as he stepped onto the stage of the "America's Got Talent" finale. Commissioned by his wife, this piece of home was by his side as he wowed the audience. At the finale, 27-year-old Wu, from Sichuan Province in southwestern China, shared the stage with humanoid robots made by Unitree, performing in a fusion of robotics, ink-wash aesthetics, and contemporary stage performance. "Robots are not merely technological achievements, but can also become creative partners on stage and a new medium for artistic expression," said Fang Zhenghua, the Chengdu choreographer who directed the team's performances. Wu said their experience in the United States has been genuinely heartwarming. He, along with Fang, showcased not only the advances in humanoid robot technology, but also young people's vision of the future relationship between technology and humanity, adding that audiences are incredibly enthusiastic. At their audition, Wu performed alongside machines that danced and flipped in time with the music. The act received a unanimous yes from all four judges. By the Sept. 8 quarterfinals, Wu and the robots were performing martial arts alongside human dancers, kicking and flipping across the stage. Judge Howie Mandel imagined a martial arts version of the film "I, Robot" and predicted it would be "the most viral moment we're going to have this season." Actress Sofia Vergara pressed her Golden Buzzer, sending the team directly to the Sept. 22 final. For Wu, however, some of the most memorable exchanges happened away from the machines. This marked his fourth trip to the United States. He had met a number of American dancers on past trips from the East Coast to the West Coast of the country. They made dance videos together on American streets, capturing times when they moved and played music together. "Dance is a universal language," he said. When he made it to the finale, some of those friends reached out on social media to wish him luck. He also received encouraging messages from local viewers he had never met. "Even though we come from different countries and speak different languages, at that moment they were sincerely wishing me well in the competition," Wu said. "That stayed with me. It felt quite warm." Wu grew up visiting the Sanxingdui Ruins, a site associated with the ancient Shu Kingdom dating back some 3,000 to 4,500 years. He said visiting the site was "like going to a park." During the contest, he brought one of those familiar faces across the Pacific, jokingly calling it a "mysterious force from the East." For Fang, inspiration also comes from familiar stories and everyday life. Over the years, his team has incorporated elements like Sichuan opera face-changing, the traditional Chinese composition "A Hundred Birds Paying Homage to the Phoenix," and Three Kingdoms stories into the performances. For the finale, choreographer Fang wanted to share a Chinese aesthetic that overseas audiences might know less well than kung fu. Water sleeves offered one way to do that, with robots becoming partners in expressing an old art form. Wu's appearance came in a year when American audiences encountered Chinese creativity in several different settings. In July, Chinese artists joined the Hollywood Film Music Orchestra for a "Black Myth: Wukong" concert in Los Angeles, while Lincoln Center expanded its previous Shanghai Day celebration into Chinese Arts Week. September brought Chinese dance dramas, including "Dream of the Red Chamber," to New York. On the final stage, flowing sleeves and humanoid robots brought something of China to American viewers, and the friendship had also become part of the story that Wu and his performers would take back home. ■

item.title: China launches anti-dumping probe into EU p-Nitrotoluene imports
item.description:
Published: 2026-10-03
BEIJING, Oct. 3 (Xinhua) -- China has launched an anti-dumping investigation into imports of p-Nitrotoluene from the European Union (EU), the Ministry of Commerce said Saturday. According to the ministry's statement, it received a formal application on Sept. 14, 2026, from two domestic producers representing China's p-Nitrotoluene industry, requesting an anti-dumping investigation into imports from the EU. In response to a media query, a ministry spokesperson said preliminary evidence submitted by the applicants showed that the volume of p-Nitrotoluene imports from the EU remained at a high level from 2022 to 2025, with prices falling by nearly 60 percent cumulatively over the period. The dumped imports from the EU caused damage to the production and operations of China's domestic industry, the spokesperson said. The spokesperson pointed out that the application met the requirements for initiating an anti-dumping investigation under Chinese law and World Trade Organization rules, adding that China will conduct the investigation in accordance with relevant laws and regulations, fully protect the rights of all interested parties, and render an objective and impartial ruling. Noting that China has consistently taken a prudent and restrained approach to trade remedy measures, the spokesperson said the EU has launched 28 trade remedy investigations against China since 2025, about half of them involving chemical products, including three recent consecutive investigations into Chinese chemical products such as polyvinyl chloride. China has repeatedly called on the EU to face up to its own economic and trade issues and address each other's concerns through dialogue and consultation, the spokesperson said. According to the statement, the investigation began on Saturday and is expected to conclude before Oct. 3, 2027. It may be extended by six months under special circumstances. P-Nitrotoluene, also known as 4-Nitrotoluene, is mainly used to produce chemicals that are widely applied in dyes, pigments, pesticides, and pharmaceuticals, according to the ministry. ■

item.title: 90 years on, Long March stories resonate across generations and borders
item.description:
Published: 2026-10-03
GUIYANG, Oct. 3 (Xinhua) -- Standing before a grave marked "Red Army Tomb" in Zunyi, a city in southwest China's Guizhou Province, Kong Xia told visitors about the young medic buried beneath it. The medic was only 18 years old in January 1935, when the Red Army reached Zunyi during the Long March. Staying behind to treat sick villagers, he lost contact with his unit and was killed by enemy forces. Local people, risking their own lives, secretly buried the body. A foreign listener once told her before the tomb: "A good deed is remembered, even a hundred years later." For Kong Xia, a 56-year-old volunteer who has told Long March stories for more than three decades, the words capture something universal. The feelings the Long March evokes -- kindness, perseverance, longing for a good life -- belong to no single language or nation. Ninety years after the epic journey, the stories are finding new listeners and inspiring people in their everyday lives. The Red Army, led by the Communist Party of China (CPC), was mainly made up of soldiers from peasants' and workers' families during the Chinese revolution. Between 1934 and 1936, the army trekked up to 12,500 kilometers to break through the Kuomintang party (KMT) siege, a journey later known as the Long March. It was no easy journey. The army went through more than 600 battles while braving raging rivers, snow-covered mountains, and treacherous grasslands, with many dying on the way. By December 1934, less than two months into the march, the Central Red Army had lost more than half its strength, shrinking from over 86,000 to just over 30,000. Known as China's "city of historic turning point," Zunyi holds a special place in the nation's history. In January 1935, after arriving, the CPC convened a three-day meeting to draw lessons from the loss, which ultimately corrected the army's strategic mistakes and established a new Party leadership with Mao Zedong at the helm. About a month later, the Red Army won its first major victory of the march at Loushan Pass in Zunyi, proving the new strategy was working. The foundation laid in the mountainous city would carry the Chinese revolution to eventual victory. Kong Xia's grandfather, Kong Xianquan, a Red Army staff officer, witnessed the great transformation. Storming the pass with his unit, the then 24-year-old was shot in the right leg. When he died in 1988, six pieces of shrapnel were found among his ashes. His comrade, Zhong Chibing, badly wounded in the same battle, underwent three amputations without anesthetic as repeated infections set in under poor sanitary conditions. Rather than recuperate, the young man insisted on staying with the army and completed the Long March on one leg. Their stories capture the resilience that defined Red Army soldiers: a refusal to let hardship stand in the way of the cause they believed in. Born in 1911 to a peasant family in Liuyang, central China's Hunan Province, Kong Xianquan joined the revolution for a simple reason. He wanted enough food to eat. He also wanted to find an army that did not bully people like the KMT troops. So he joined a peasant armed force in 1928, and then in 1930, the Red Army. In 1954, Kong Xianquan became the first curator of the Zunyi Meeting memorial hall. Despite his wounded leg, the veteran traveled across mountains and valleys, collecting more than 1,200 precious artifacts for the memorial. "My grandfather spoke less, but when he told stories of the past, he was always excited," Kong Xia told Xinhua in an interview. "He never kept an account of his own deeds. What he cared about was how to record history, so that those who came after could truly see the road they had traveled." Today, Kong Xia has taken up her grandfather's baton to tell Long March stories. Since 1993, she has given more than 1,000 voluntary lectures to over 50,000 listeners, and has trained hundreds of young docents. Now retired, she continues to find new ways to bring these stories to younger generations. The year 2026 marks the 90th anniversary of the Long March victory, also the start of China's 15th Five-Year Plan period (2026-2030). The next five years will be a critical stage for the country to advance toward its goal of basically realizing socialist modernization by 2035. Kong Xia believes the Long March spirit, which comes down to keeping the faith, braving setback after setback, and putting the people first, is important to achieving the Chinese dream. "When people tell the Long March stories today, they do not tell to dwell on misery, but to light the way forward," she said. The Long March is never a story told merely within China. First published in Britain in 1937, American journalist Edgar Snow's "Red Star Over China" introduced the Chinese revolution to international readers. Decades later, Pulitzer Prize-winning journalist Harrison Salisbury retraced the route and described the Long March as "a great human epic." This year, Kong Xia has seen a growing number of foreign visitors at the memorial hall and other historical sites in Zunyi. She attributes the rise to China's prosperity and stability. "They come with questions: Why did China succeed in the past? Will it continue to succeed? I believe there will be even more foreign visitors in the future. Because as other countries develop, China's experience may serve as a reference," she added. Ninety years on, the Long March stories are still being told. And for Kong Xia, these stories are worth telling for a lifetime, and the spirit in the stories will keep traveling -- to new listeners, in new languages, and for years to come. ■

item.title: Extended breaks, richer experiences add momentum to China's holiday travel boom
item.description:
Published: 2026-10-03
BEIJING, Oct. 3 (Xinhua) -- China's National Day travel market kicked off on a strong note, as many travelers linked the Mid-Autumn Festival and National Day breaks with their annual leave. This trend has led to longer trips and a surge in bookings for long-haul journeys, multi-city itineraries and experience-based travel products. LONGER BREAKS, FARTHER JOURNEYS With the Mid-Autumn Festival and National Day separated by only three working days this year, some travelers used three days of leave to link the two breaks into a 13-day holiday. Trip.com Group data showed that one in every 10 travelers combined the two holidays into an extended break. Cao Shuai, CEO of Tongcheng Travel's destination business division, said strong demand for the 13-day break has lengthened the overall consumption cycle and helped release demand for long-haul and in-depth travel. Data from online travel platform Qunar showed that by Oct. 1, the first day of the National Day holiday, 20 percent of travelers had already reached the second city on their itineraries. Nearly 30 percent had booked hotels in at least two cities, while bookings involving stays in four or more cities surged 53 percent year on year. For Yuan You, who works for an internet company, the 13-day break made it possible to split one holiday into two distinct stages. She planned to first spend three days in Jiuzhaigou, a UNESCO-listed scenic area in southwest China's Sichuan Province known for its turquoise lakes and waterfalls, before continuing to Chengdu for the remainder of the break. "With such a long break, spending the whole time either resting or sightseeing can become monotonous, so I opted for a mix of both," Yuan said. In Chengdu, she chose to spend part of that extra time learning woodworking. Longer breaks are encouraging people to travel farther. Flight bookings for journeys of more than 2,000 km rose 76 percent year on year during the Mid-Autumn Festival and National Day period, accounting for more than a quarter of all flight bookings, according to Meituan. Wang Peng, an associate researcher at the Beijing Academy of Social Sciences, said the extended break has encouraged more people to start traveling earlier, spreading trips over a longer period rather than concentrating them within a few peak days. That, Wang said, could help sustain demand across tourism, accommodation and catering services for longer periods of time. China State Railway Group Co., Ltd. (China Railway) said that China's railway network handled 25.204 million passenger trips on Oct. 1, setting a new single-day record. RICHER EXPERIENCES, MORE TO EXPLORE The surge in mobility has translated into demand for richer experiences at destinations. At the National Maritime Museum of China in north China's Tianjin Municipality, 19,000 visitors streamed through the doors on the opening day of the National Day break. Among the new draws is "Echoes of the Whale Song," the museum's first customized full-sensory virtual reality experience. Unlike conventional walk-through VR attractions, visitors remain seated as the experience unfolds around them, allowing for a more immersive encounter. Under blue lights, visitors see a giant whale entangled in discarded fishing nets and take part in a virtual rescue, learning along the way about the impact of marine debris on ocean life. Such experience-oriented products are gaining traction well beyond one museum. On Fliggy, Alibaba Group's online travel platform, domestic attraction ticket bookings on Oct. 1 rose nearly 30 percent year on year, while the number of users purchasing products for natural scenic areas and villages increased by nearly 50 percent. Searches on Qunar for "immersive performances," "fireworks shows" and "night tours" also climbed more than 50 percent year on year. The growing demand for interactive travel experiences can be seen at Changchun Zoological and Botanical Park in northeast China's Jilin Province. There, a nighttime immersive show inspired by the Chinese classic "Journey to the West" has drawn large crowds into a vibrant fantasy world, with costumed performers mingling with visitors and transforming the park into a stage after dark. Yang Han, a researcher with Qunar's big data research institute, said travelers are increasingly setting out to "enter a story" rather than simply view static scenery, with content-driven experiences gaining popularity and bringing new opportunities to less traditional tourism destinations. Bu Xiting, an associate researcher in the School of Cultural Industries Management at Communication University of China, contrasted the current trend with the previously popular "special forces-style tourism," a fast-paced form of travel in which people try to pack as many sights as possible into a short period, and city walks, which offer smaller-scale urban experiences during pockets of free time. By linking public holidays with annual leave, travelers now have more time to shape their trips around what they want to experience, Bu said. Tourism consumption, Bu noted, is shifting from a focus on "time efficiency" toward greater "experience density." ■

item.title: Xi calls for firm confidence, solid steps for China's national rejuvenation
item.description:
Published: 2026-09-30
Chinese President Xi Jinping, also general secretary of the Communist Party of China Central Committee and chairman of the Central Military Commission, delivers an important speech at a reception to celebrate the 77th anniversary of the founding of the People's Republic of China at the Great Hall of the People in Beijing, capital of China, Sept. 30, 2026. (Xinhua/Xie Huanchi) BEIJING, Sept. 30 (Xinhua) -- Chinese President Xi Jinping on Wednesday called on the nation to forge ahead with firm confidence and take solid steps to achieve the great national rejuvenation. Xi, also general secretary of the Communist Party of China (CPC) Central Committee and chairman of the Central Military Commission, made the remarks at a reception held at the Great Hall of the People in Beijing to celebrate the 77th anniversary of the founding of the People's Republic of China. China's National Day falls on Oct. 1. Li Qiang presided over the reception. Zhao Leji, Wang Huning, Cai Qi, Ding Xuexiang, Li Xi and Han Zheng attended the event along with around 800 guests. "The great rejuvenation of the Chinese nation is unstoppable," Xi said. "As long as we remain confident, stay focused on our goals and move forward steadily, step by step, success will ultimately belong to the great CPC, the great Chinese people and the great People's Republic of China." He noted that over the past 77 years, the Party has led the Chinese people in achieving two miracles: rapid economic growth and enduring social stability. "We take immense pride in the extraordinary achievements of New China and have full confidence in the bright prospects of Chinese modernization," he said. Since the beginning of this year, the Chinese economy has continued to progress despite mounting pressure and achieved innovation-driven and high-quality development, demonstrating strong resilience and vitality, he said. Efforts should be made to sustain this momentum, promote innovation-driven, high-quality and sound economic development, take practical steps to safeguard and improve people's livelihoods, and meet the targets and tasks set for the year, so as to ensure a good start to the 15th Five-Year Plan (2026-2030), he said. Xi stressed the need to remain firmly committed to the policy of "one country, two systems," under which the people of Hong Kong administer Hong Kong, the people of Macao administer Macao, and both regions enjoy a high degree of autonomy. He went on to say that the central government will support Hong Kong and Macao in integrating more fully into the country's overall development. The central government is committed to maintaining their long-term prosperity and stability, Xi added. He also called for efforts to deepen exchanges and cooperation across the Taiwan Strait, resolutely fight secessionist forces seeking "Taiwan independence," oppose external interference, and promote the peaceful development of cross-Strait relations to advance national reunification. China will stick to its independent foreign policy of peace, advance the implementation of the four major global initiatives it proposed, and promote the building of a community with a shared future for humanity to contribute greater certainty and positive energy to a turbulent world, Xi said. ■ The Communist Party of China and state leaders Xi Jinping, Li Qiang, Zhao Leji, Wang Huning, Cai Qi, Ding Xuexiang, Li Xi and Han Zheng attend a reception to celebrate the 77th anniversary of the founding of the People's Republic of China along with around 800 guests at the Great Hall of the People in Beijing, capital of China, Sept. 30, 2026.
